screens.title: What is a Rollup?
screens.narratorSegment: A rollup is a Layer 2 scaling construct that executes transactions off-chain, bundles them into a batch, and posts a compressed summary and a cryptographic proof to Layer 1. The important claim to understand is that the L1 does not re-execute every transaction; instead it verifies a small on-chain artifact, which is enough to inherit the L1's security properties. A rollup posts either full transaction data, a compressed form, or at least a commitment to that data on L1 — this is data availability. Data availability lets anyone reconstruct the off-chain state and verify the rollup's transitions, even if the rollup operator goes offline. A common misconception is thinking that processing off-chain eliminates on-chain trust guarantees; it does not. The proof and posted data are the bridge that keeps L1 security. For example, a rollup can take hundreds of transfers, compute a new state root, and submit that root plus a proof. L1 verifies the proof and the commitment, so users know they can recover funds. Key takeaway: rollups shift execution off-chain for throughput but rely on L1 commitments for integrity and recoverability.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Rollups bundle off-chain transactions and post a compact proof or commitment to L1 so the chain can verify correctness without processing every transaction.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › What is a Rollup?
Definition

Rollup mechanics

Execute off-chain, bundle many transactions, compute a new state root, and post a proof or optimistic batch plus data commitment to Layer 1.

Data availability: posting transaction data or a commitment on L1 so others can reconstruct state.
Integrity: L1 verifies a proof or processes a fraud proof to maintain correctness.
Throughput: Many off-chain transactions are compressed into one L1 verification step.
Key Takeaway

Rollups increase throughput by off-loading execution while keeping L1 as the trust root through commitments and proofs.

Analogy
Think of a rollup like a batch courier: many letters packaged into a single parcel with a seal. L1 checks the seal rather than every letter.
  • What it proves: the correctness of the new state root after applying the batch.
  • Why it matters: reduces on-chain computation and gas while preserving safety.
  • Misconception to avoid: off-chain does not mean unprotected; commitments preserve security.
Concrete example
Hundreds of transfers are applied off-chain, producing a single new state root and a proof. L1 validates that root or accepts a fraud proof within a challenge window.

screens.title: How an Optimistic Rollup Works
screens.narratorSegment: Optimistic Rollups work by assuming that the sequencer submits valid batches, then relying on the community to challenge any invalid state transition. The sequencer collects transactions, orders them, and posts a batch with a commitment and metadata to Layer 1. Once posted, a challenge period begins — often on the order of days — during which anyone may submit a fraud proof if they detect an invalid transaction or incorrect state transition in the batch. If a valid fraud proof is proven on L1, the invalid batch is reverted and the sequencer may be penalized. A concrete example: suppose a sequencer posts a batch that incorrectly credits an address. A watcher node notices the inconsistency, constructs a fraud proof demonstrating the faulty state transition, and submits it within the challenge window. The L1 contract verifies the fraud proof and reverts the bad batch. A common mistake is assuming instant withdrawals; optimistic designs require waiting for the challenge window to pass because finality is conditional until the window closes. Key takeaway: optimistic rollups trade a simpler proof model for a withdrawal delay that enforces correctness via economic incentives and public contestability.

screens.title: Optimistic vs ZK-Rollups — Security Models
screens.narratorSegment: Optimistic and ZK-Rollups secure batches in very different ways. Optimistic designs assume the batch is valid and allow a challenge period for fraud proofs. The security is social and economic: watchers must monitor chains and submit fraud proofs to correct bad behavior. ZK-Rollups, on the other hand, attach a cryptographic validity proof to each batch. This proof mathematically guarantees that the new state root follows from the prior root and the included transactions. The result is immediate finality once the proof is verified on L1. A concrete contrast: in an optimistic rollup, a user who withdraws funds to L1 must wait through the challenge period because a fraud proof could still reverse the batch. With a ZK-Rollup, the verified proof makes withdrawals instant because the computation correctness is cryptographically established. A common misconception is that ZK is always superior; it's stronger in finality but often imposes higher computational costs and complexity for developers. The right choice depends on the application's tolerance for withdrawal delay versus cryptographic and runtime overhead. Optimistic vs ZK-Rollups — Security Models means optimistic uses contestability and fraud proofs; zk uses cryptographic validity proofs that give instant finality after verification.. In practical terms, compare assumptions: fraud proofs and validity proofs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Optimistic vs ZK
Optimistic

Assume then challenge

Batches are assumed valid. Watchers submit fraud proofs during a challenge period to revert invalid batches. Simpler proof logic; withdrawal delay required.

EVM friendly and easier to port existing dApps.
Risk: users must wait for challenge windows before final L1 settlement.
ZK-Rollup

Validity proofs give instant finality

Each batch comes with a zero-knowledge validity proof that the state transition is correct. L1 verifies the proof and accepts the batch immediately.

Immediate withdrawals and strong cryptographic guarantees.
Trade-off: higher computational overhead and cryptographic complexity.
Key Takeaway

Choose optimistic for developer ease and EVM compatibility; choose ZK when immediate finality and cryptographic guarantees are required despite higher complexity.

screens.title: Sequencer and Data Availability
screens.narratorSegment: Two operational pieces power a rollup: the sequencer and data availability commitments. The sequencer aggregates, orders, and signs batches before submission. If sequencer behavior is malicious or buggy, the posted commitments and the rollup's dispute or proof process enable recovery. Data availability is the principle that transaction data, or a verifiable commitment to it, is published on Layer 1 so third parties can reconstruct the off-chain ledger. This prevents censorship and preserves the user's ability to withdraw funds even if the sequencer goes offline. For example, if the sequencer stops producing batches, nodes can read the posted data and rebuild the state from the last confirmed root. A common mistake is underestimating the importance of complete data availability; posting only a small commitment without sufficient data can prevent state reconstruction. In practice, rollups choose whether to post full calldata, compressed calldata, or commitments, balancing gas cost with reconstructibility guarantees. Sequencer and Data Availability means sequencers perform batching and ordering; data availability on l1 ensures anyone can rebuild state and prevents censorship or loss of funds.. In practical terms, roles, commitments, and reconstructibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Sequencer & Data Availability
Components

Sequencer role

Orders transactions, forms batches, and submits commitments to L1. Sequencer incentives and penalties help align honest behavior.

If sequencer behaves badly, fraud proofs or invalidity proofs allow correction.
Some rollups decentralize sequencer duties to reduce trust assumptions.
Data Availability

Why publish data to L1?

Posting transaction data or commitments lets watchers reconstruct state and prevents censorship, even if operators go offline.

  • Full calldata on L1: strongest reconstructibility but higher gas cost.
  • Commitment-only: cheaper but requires additional trust or data-availability layers.
Key Takeaway

Data availability choices determine how easily third parties can reconstruct rollup state and recover user funds if operators fail.

screens.title: Fraud Proofs and the Challenge Period
screens.narratorSegment: Fraud proofs in optimistic rollups are evidence that a posted batch produced an invalid state transition. Conceptually, a fraud proof demonstrates that applying a specific transaction or set of transactions to the prior state root would not produce the submitted new state root. The challenge period exists so watchers have time to construct and submit these proofs. Without a challenge period, a bad batch could be settled on L1 immediately, leaving users unable to recover funds if the batch contains fraud. A concrete example: if a transaction duplicates funds or misapplies a balance change, a fraud proof will show the precise contradiction and L1 logic will revert the batch when the proof verifies. Common mistakes include misreading the challenge period as optional; it is the core mechanism that makes optimistic designs work. Another misconception is equating fraud proofs with validity proofs — fraud proofs assert a mistake after the fact and require a window to be effective, while validity proofs preemptively guarantee correctness. Think of fraud proofs as a safety net that requires time to deploy. Fraud Proofs and the Challenge Period means fraud proofs demonstrate incorrect state transitions during the challenge window and are essential for optimistic rollup security.. In practical terms, what fraud proofs prove and why the challenge window exists. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › Fraud Proofs
What it proves

Invalid state transition

A fraud proof shows that applying the posted transactions to the previous state would not produce the submitted new state root, demonstrating a fault.

  • Requires sufficient evidence: inputs, receipts, and a verifiable mismatch.
  • Submitted to L1 during the challenge window for on-chain verification.
Why the challenge period
It gives watchers time to detect, build, and submit fraud proofs. Without it, incorrect batches could finalize immediately on L1.
Common misconception: fraud proofs are not pre-emptive guarantees. They are reactive and require time to be effective.
Key Takeaway

Fraud proofs plus a challenge period create the contestable security model that allows optimistic rollups to be simpler at the cost of delayed finality.

screens.title: Validity Proofs and Zero-Knowledge Rollups
screens.narratorSegment: ZK-Rollups attach a cryptographic validity proof to every batch. A zero-knowledge proof demonstrates that the new state root is the correct result of applying the included transactions to the previous state — and it does so without revealing extra transaction internals. Once the L1 contract verifies this validity proof, the batch is accepted and its state becomes final on L1. The practical consequence is faster withdrawals and immediate finality because no challenge window is needed. A concrete example: if a batch contains three transfers, the ZK proof certifies that applying those transfers to the previous root produces the new root. A common misconception is that zero-knowledge implies secrecy of everything; in rollups, the ZKP proves correctness while posted data or commitments still provide data availability. The trade-off is computational: generating proofs can be resource intensive and require specialized circuit design. The key insight is that ZK-Rollups replace contestability with mathematical guarantees, shortening the path to finality at higher engineering cost. Validity Proofs and Zero-Knowledge Rollups means zero-knowledge validity proofs cryptographically guarantee a batch's correctness, enabling immediate finality on l1 without a challenge window.. In practical terms, what a zkp proves and why finality is immediate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.3 › ZK-Rollup Validity Proofs
What the ZKP proves

Correct state computation

The proof certifies that the new state root matches the application of the transactions to the previous state root. L1 verifies the proof and finality is immediate.

Does not remove data availability — rollups still post data or commitments so state is reconstructible.
Proof generation is computationally expensive and requires circuit design expertise.
Concrete example
A batch with three transfers is accompanied by a ZK validity proof that mathematically guarantees the resulting state root is correct. The L1 contract verifies this and accepts the batch instantly.
Key Takeaway

ZK-Rollups use cryptographic proofs for immediate finality, trading lower latency for higher proof-generation complexity.

screens.title: Trade-offs: Withdrawal Times, Overhead, and Compatibility
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between optimistic and ZK rollups requires weighing withdrawal latency, computational overhead, and how easy it is to reuse existing tooling. Optimistic rollups tend to be easier to implement for EVM-based dApps because they don't require building complex cryptographic circuits; they favor developer experience and compatibility. The trade-off is a withdrawal delay due to the challenge period. ZK-Rollups, by contrast, offer immediate finality and fast withdrawals since the validity proof settles correctness instantly. screens.title: Batch Example: Compute Final Balances
screens.narratorSegment: Let's work through a concrete batch example to solidify how rollups update balances and how proofs support that update. Start with the initial L1 state: Alice 100, Bob 50, Carol 20 — total 170. The rollup processes three off-chain transactions: Alice sends 10 to Bob; Bob sends 5 to Carol; Carol sends 3 to Alice. After these transactions, Alice's balance changes by minus 10 then plus 3, resulting in 93. Bob gains 10 then loses 5, resulting in 55. Carol gains 5 then pays 3, resulting in 22. Total supply remains 170, which is a quick consistency check. The batch includes previousStateRoot and newStateRoot that act as cryptographic commitments. The proof attached to the batch — a fraud proof in optimistic systems or a validity proof in ZK systems — is what the L1 uses to accept or contest the newStateRoot. Conceptually, a fraud proof argues that applying a particular transaction will not produce the new root, while a validity proof certifies the computation did produce the new root. As a takeaway, always verify total supply consistency and know what the proof asserts before trusting finality. Which account would you audit first if an imbalance appears?

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Watcher Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Watchers are third-party nodes or services that monitor rollup submissions to detect invalid batches. A frequent pitfall is underestimating the operational need for active watchers in optimistic rollups; if nobody watches, fraud proofs won't be submitted and invalid batches could remain unchallenged. Teams may also misconfigure data publication and fail to provide sufficient data availability, making reconstructibility impossible if operators stop responding. Developers sometimes assume instant L1 finality after a batch post; for optimistic rollups this is false until the challenge period expires. For ZK-rollups, a common mistake is underestimating proof-generation time and costs, leading to slow batch cadence or bottlenecks. Watchers should verify consistency of state roots, check that posted calldata is complete, and alert on anomalies. The practical advice is to instrument monitoring, plan for penalties and incentives, and design recovery steps if the sequencer fails. Reflect: how would you ensure a reliable watcher network for an optimistic rollup production deployment? fullNarratorScript:
Today we're examining rollups, a vital Layer 2 pattern that executes transactions off-chain, compresses them, and posts a proof and data commitment to Layer 1. You will learn why rollups improve throughput dramatically without relaxing L1 security, and how two distinct approaches — optimistic and zero-knowledge — enforce correctness. I will walk you through the core mechanics: data availability commitments, the role of a sequencer that bundles transactions, and the two security models. We'll compare their practical trade-offs: withdrawal delay versus proof-generation cost, and developer experience when targeting EVM compatibility. To ground this, imagine three simple transfers bundled into a single batch — the L1 only needs to verify a small proof or wait for a challenge window, not every transfer. That design is why rollups scale. Watch for the common misconception that off-chain processing removes L1 guarantees; it does not, because the rollup posts essential data or commitments on-chain. As you explore the chapter, ask: which rollup style matches my application's needs — instant finality with more cryptographic work, or familiar tooling with challenge windows?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define what a rollup is, distinguish the two main security models used in rollups, explain how fraud proofs and challenge periods operate, and analyze the trade-offs between withdrawal latency, proof cost, and developer compatibility. First, you will understand the rollup pattern: off-chain execution, on-chain commitments, and an on-chain verification step. Next, you will compare Optimistic and ZK-Rollups: Optimistic uses fraud proofs and a challenge window, while ZK-Rollups rely on validity proofs and cryptographic finality. Third, you will explain how sequencers and data availability interact so anyone can reconstruct state if needed. Finally, you will evaluate when a team should pick an Optimistic approach for EVM ease versus a ZK approach for instant finality. Each objective is paired with a practical mnemonic or visual to help you remember the security trade-offs and operational implications for real dApps.

These objectives focus on applying rollup knowledge in design choices. You'll practice calculating final balances from a batch, explaining the role of state roots and proofs, and identifying whether a project should prefer optimistic or ZK approaches. You will also learn to spot misconceptions: for example, believing that off-chain execution means weaker L1 security. Instead, strong security comes from posting commitments or proofs on L1 and maintaining data availability. Finally, you'll be able to reason about sequencer trust and how penalty mechanisms or open challenge windows reduce the risk of fraud. Each objective ties to a verified competency milestone so you can self-check your understanding with concrete examples and a guided batch exercise later in the chapter. Learning Objectives — Applied Skills means translate rollup mechanisms into design decisions: proof type, withdrawal policy, and developer tooling when choosing an l2 strategy.. In practical terms, how to use rollup concepts in design decisions. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A rollup is a Layer 2 scaling construct that executes transactions off-chain, bundles them into a batch, and posts a compressed summary and a cryptographic proof to Layer 1. The important claim to understand is that the L1 does not re-execute every transaction; instead it verifies a small on-chain artifact, which is enough to inherit the L1's security properties. A rollup posts either full transaction data, a compressed form, or at least a commitment to that data on L1 — this is data availability. Data availability lets anyone reconstruct the off-chain state and verify the rollup's transitions, even if the rollup operator goes offline. A common misconception is thinking that processing off-chain eliminates on-chain trust guarantees; it does not. The proof and posted data are the bridge that keeps L1 security. For example, a rollup can take hundreds of transfers, compute a new state root, and submit that root plus a proof. L1 verifies the proof and the commitment, so users know they can recover funds. Key takeaway: rollups shift execution off-chain for throughput but rely on L1 commitments for integrity and recoverability.

Optimistic Rollups work by assuming that the sequencer submits valid batches, then relying on the community to challenge any invalid state transition. The sequencer collects transactions, orders them, and posts a batch with a commitment and metadata to Layer 1. Once posted, a challenge period begins — often on the order of days — during which anyone may submit a fraud proof if they detect an invalid transaction or incorrect state transition in the batch. If a valid fraud proof is proven on L1, the invalid batch is reverted and the sequencer may be penalized. A concrete example: suppose a sequencer posts a batch that incorrectly credits an address. A watcher node notices the inconsistency, constructs a fraud proof demonstrating the faulty state transition, and submits it within the challenge window. The L1 contract verifies the fraud proof and reverts the bad batch. A common mistake is assuming instant withdrawals; optimistic designs require waiting for the challenge window to pass because finality is conditional until the window closes. Key takeaway: optimistic rollups trade a simpler proof model for a withdrawal delay that enforces correctness via economic incentives and public contestability.

Optimistic and ZK-Rollups secure batches in very different ways. Optimistic designs assume the batch is valid and allow a challenge period for fraud proofs. The security is social and economic: watchers must monitor chains and submit fraud proofs to correct bad behavior. ZK-Rollups, on the other hand, attach a cryptographic validity proof to each batch. This proof mathematically guarantees that the new state root follows from the prior root and the included transactions. The result is immediate finality once the proof is verified on L1. A concrete contrast: in an optimistic rollup, a user who withdraws funds to L1 must wait through the challenge period because a fraud proof could still reverse the batch. With a ZK-Rollup, the verified proof makes withdrawals instant because the computation correctness is cryptographically established. A common misconception is that ZK is always superior; it's stronger in finality but often imposes higher computational costs and complexity for developers. The right choice depends on the application's tolerance for withdrawal delay versus cryptographic and runtime overhead. Optimistic vs ZK-Rollups — Security Models means optimistic uses contestability and fraud proofs; zk uses cryptographic validity proofs that give instant finality after verification.. In practical terms, compare assumptions: fraud proofs and validity proofs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Two operational pieces power a rollup: the sequencer and data availability commitments. The sequencer aggregates, orders, and signs batches before submission. If sequencer behavior is malicious or buggy, the posted commitments and the rollup's dispute or proof process enable recovery. Data availability is the principle that transaction data, or a verifiable commitment to it, is published on Layer 1 so third parties can reconstruct the off-chain ledger. This prevents censorship and preserves the user's ability to withdraw funds even if the sequencer goes offline. For example, if the sequencer stops producing batches, nodes can read the posted data and rebuild the state from the last confirmed root. A common mistake is underestimating the importance of complete data availability; posting only a small commitment without sufficient data can prevent state reconstruction. In practice, rollups choose whether to post full calldata, compressed calldata, or commitments, balancing gas cost with reconstructibility guarantees. Sequencer and Data Availability means sequencers perform batching and ordering; data availability on l1 ensures anyone can rebuild state and prevents censorship or loss of funds.. In practical terms, roles, commitments, and reconstructibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Fraud proofs in optimistic rollups are evidence that a posted batch produced an invalid state transition. Conceptually, a fraud proof demonstrates that applying a specific transaction or set of transactions to the prior state root would not produce the submitted new state root. The challenge period exists so watchers have time to construct and submit these proofs. Without a challenge period, a bad batch could be settled on L1 immediately, leaving users unable to recover funds if the batch contains fraud. A concrete example: if a transaction duplicates funds or misapplies a balance change, a fraud proof will show the precise contradiction and L1 logic will revert the batch when the proof verifies. Common mistakes include misreading the challenge period as optional; it is the core mechanism that makes optimistic designs work. Another misconception is equating fraud proofs with validity proofs — fraud proofs assert a mistake after the fact and require a window to be effective, while validity proofs preemptively guarantee correctness. Think of fraud proofs as a safety net that requires time to deploy. Fraud Proofs and the Challenge Period means fraud proofs demonstrate incorrect state transitions during the challenge window and are essential for optimistic rollup security.. ZK-Rollups attach a cryptographic validity proof to every batch. A zero-knowledge proof demonstrates that the new state root is the correct result of applying the included transactions to the previous state — and it does so without revealing extra transaction internals. Once the L1 contract verifies this validity proof, the batch is accepted and its state becomes final on L1. The practical consequence is faster withdrawals and immediate finality because no challenge window is needed. A concrete example: if a batch contains three transfers, the ZK proof certifies that applying those transfers to the previous root produces the new root. A common misconception is that zero-knowledge implies secrecy of everything; in rollups, the ZKP proves correctness while posted data or commitments still provide data availability. The trade-off is computational: generating proofs can be resource intensive and require specialized circuit design. The key insight is that ZK-Rollups replace contestability with mathematical guarantees, shortening the path to finality at higher engineering cost. Choosing between optimistic and ZK rollups requires weighing withdrawal latency, computational overhead, and how easy it is to reuse existing tooling. Optimistic rollups tend to be easier to implement for EVM-based dApps because they don't require building complex cryptographic circuits; they favor developer experience and compatibility. The trade-off is a withdrawal delay due to the challenge period. ZK-Rollups, by contrast, offer immediate finality and fast withdrawals since the validity proof settles correctness instantly. But they incur heavier computation for proof generation and often need specialized tooling or ZK-EVM solutions to achieve parity with existing smart contracts. For teams unfamiliar with advanced cryptography, optimistic rollups are often a practical first step. For applications requiring instant withdrawals or strict finality, ZK approaches will be preferable despite the higher engineering cost. A misconception to avoid is thinking one model is strictly better; instead, match the model to requirements: immediate finality versus developer productivity and ecosystem compatibility. Watchers are third-party nodes or services that monitor rollup submissions to detect invalid batches. A frequent pitfall is underestimating the operational need for active watchers in optimistic rollups; if nobody watches, fraud proofs won't be submitted and invalid batches could remain unchallenged. Teams may also misconfigure data publication and fail to provide sufficient data availability, making reconstructibility impossible if operators stop responding. Developers sometimes assume instant L1 finality after a batch post; for optimistic rollups this is false until the challenge period expires. For ZK-rollups, a common mistake is underestimating proof-generation time and costs, leading to slow batch cadence or bottlenecks. Watchers should verify consistency of state roots, check that posted calldata is complete, and alert on anomalies. The practical advice is to instrument monitoring, plan for penalties and incentives, and design recovery steps if the sequencer fails. When selecting a rollup approach, use a short checklist to align technical requirements and team capabilities. First, ask whether immediate withdrawals and instant L1 finality are essential. If yes, ZK-Rollups are typically the correct choice because validity proofs remove the need for a challenge window. Second, assess your team's familiarity with cryptography and circuit construction. If your team prefers working with existing EVM tooling and wants a shorter ramp, optimistic rollups are more practical. Third, consider throughput and latency — both rollups improve throughput, but operational cadence differs depending on proof generation time and batch frequency. Fourth, evaluate data availability strategy and cost: posting full calldata is safer but more expensive. Finally, think about who will run watchers and how penalties or incentives will be enforced.
